headline.label: Overall usability score
headline.sentence: Team plan onboarding looks a little below target, but six people are too few to tell for sure.

sections.heading: What we measured
paragraphs: Six people each tried two onboarding tasks for the team plan: Book a demo and Invite a teammate. During each call, a moderator noted whether they finished, how long it took, and how easy it felt.

A task counts as finished only if the person finished it without help. Someone who needed a hint from the moderator counts as not finished. People rated how easy each task felt from 1 to 5, where 5 means very easy. We use that rating as our measure of satisfaction.
The aim was to find the weaker of the two tasks, so the team knows where to look first.

sections.heading: Your result
paragraphs: The overall usability score is 45%. A score of 50% means exactly on target. Higher is better, and lower is worse.
The score looks a little below the 50% target, but the study cannot yet tell for sure. The likely range runs from 21% to 82%, and the target sits inside it.
Invite a teammate scored 42% and Book a demo scored 48%. For each task, we cannot yet tell whether it is above or below its target.
Invite a teammate scored lower, so it is the first candidate for the weaker task. But the two ranges overlap a lot, so this study cannot prove that it is weaker.

sections.heading: What the score is made of
paragraphs: Each task score combines three equal parts: how many people finished, how fast they were, and how easy it felt. Only the people who finished count towards time.

items.label: Book a demo: completion
items.text: Three of 6 people finished. The team set no target for this part.

items.label: Book a demo: time on task
items.text: A typical attempt took 79 seconds, against a target of 90 seconds. This part is on target.

items.label: Book a demo: satisfaction
items.text: The average ease rating was 3.17 on the 1 to 5 scale, against a target of 4. This part is off target.

items.label: Invite a teammate: completion
items.text: Three of 6 people finished. The team set no target for this part.

items.label: Invite a teammate: time on task
items.text: A typical attempt took 81 seconds, against a target of 75 seconds. This part is off target.

items.label: Invite a teammate: satisfaction
items.text: The average ease rating was 3.5 on the 1 to 5 scale, against a target of 4. This part is off target.

sections.heading: How sure we are
paragraphs: With six people, the true overall score is most likely between 21% and 82%. That range is very wide, because each person who finishes or does not finish moves the score a lot.
The task ranges are just as wide: 30% to 82% for Book a demo, and 21% to 76% for Invite a teammate. With so little data, even these ranges are only rough.
Testing more people would narrow the ranges. Only then could we say whether each task is above or below its target, and which task is really weaker.

sections.heading: What to fix first
paragraphs: For Invite a teammate, the weakest part is time. A typical attempt took 81 seconds against a target of 75 seconds. Look at which steps of inviting slow people down.
For Book a demo, the weakest part is satisfaction. People finished quickly enough, but the average ease rating was only 3.17 against a target of 4. Look at what made booking feel hard.

In each task, half of the people did not finish on their own. The moderator also noted that several people asked what "seat" means. That comes from the notes, not from a measured number, but the word is worth checking.

sections.heading: What this number cannot tell you
paragraphs: The score shows how well people did, not why they struggled. For the reasons, read the moderator's notes and watch any recordings.
A study of six people is very small, so every part of the score is uncertain. The times describe only the people who finished, because nobody else has a time recorded.
The data was copied by hand from notes typed during the calls, and the times were written as free text. The table was checked, but small copying or timing errors are still possible.
These results cover only these two tasks and these six people. Another common way of scoring gives 44%, so the choice of scoring method does not change the answer.

glossary.definition: One number that sums up how well people managed a task. 50% means exactly on target; higher is better, lower is worse.
The level the team agreed a task should reach, such as a time limit or an ease rating.
The values the true score most likely falls between. Fewer people give a wider range.
Whether a person finished the task on their own, without a hint from the moderator.
Here, the "How easy" rating each person gave after a task, from 1 to 5 where 5 means very easy.
How long a typical person who finished took to complete the task.

notes: The draft had no mechanical readability issues; edits were light polish only.
Split long sentences in "What we measured" and tightened the limits section.
Kept the verdict soft throughout: the score "looks" below target and the study "cannot yet tell for sure".
Added "Completion" to the glossary, since it labels two of the score parts.
The "seat" wording point comes from moderator notes only; a researcher should confirm it before acting on it.
